title: The reference guardrail: evaluate a prompt against devenv/reference before acting
description:
Guide a developer who is unfamiliar with a mounted library. Any starting point — vague goal, wrong API call, pasted error, design question — is checked against reference before work proceeds.

Three steps:
  1. reference is assumed correctly mounted (given)
  2. determine whether relevant information exists — the agent READS ./ch vocab (~3,900 tok for all mounted registers) rather than searching it
  3. evaluate the prompt against what it found — ./ch entry on the selected ids, plus the phrasebook and relation joins

Output for the user: what this library calls what they described; what they will also need (relation neighbours); where they contradict it (contrasts-with edges); and what it genuinely does not do.

MEASURED, and the reason this is a reading design rather than a search design: embedding retrieval over entry documents failed 4/4 on novice phrasing, with the wrongest answer scoring highest (0.81, abort controllers, for a question about cost). It also produced a FALSE GAP — 'cost and pricing' reported nothing named that, while usage-class and Collector were both present. For a guardrail a false gap is the worst error: it sends the user away from an answer that was there.

A gap verdict is only defensible when the whole vocabulary was read: 'none of the 430 things BAML names concern OAuth' is auditable by the human because the list is in context. 'Embedding returned nothing above 0.2' is not.
design:
Clarification/refinement of the prompt is explicitly OUT of scope here — this issue covers detection and evaluation only, and hands its verdict to that step.

Scales to hundreds of terms, not thousands. Past ~5,000 the read-whole-vocabulary move breaks and selection must scope by group first; the manifest already carries groups as the escape hatch.

Relation coverage is uneven — 38 of 430 BAML terms have no edges, median degree 2 — so the what-you-will-also-need guidance is only as good as the register's relations.
acceptance_criteria: Given a novice-phrased prompt about a mounted library, the guardrail names the corpus terms involved, surfaces their relation neighbourhood, flags contrasts-with conflicts, and reports true gaps; validated against the four novice prompts that broke the retrieval approach.

title: ./ch entry: batch entry resolution with phrasebook and relations pre-joined
description:
The evaluation surface for the reference guardrail. Given entry ids selected from ./ch vocab, return each one's full payload: definition, kind, aliases, anchors — plus the two deterministic joins that make it useful to an unfamiliar user.

Today ask --json returns only [{id, score}]; the content exists but renders for humans only (study._entry_lines). An agent gets ids it cannot resolve without re-reading YAML.

Joins:
  phrasebook — via each entry's terms: back-reference; carries the template: scaffolding
  relations  — via from/to; 572 edges in BAML, 392/430 terms connected, median degree 2

The relation neighbourhood is what tells an unfamiliar user what they will ALSO need (uses / part-of / configures) and where they are contradicting the library (40 contrasts-with edges in BAML).
acceptance_criteria: ./ch entry <reg> <id>... --json returns full entries plus joined phrasings and relation neighbourhood; accepts multiple ids in one call; read-only.
close_reason: ./ch entry lands: batch entry resolution with both joins pre-computed. Accepts bare slugs (what vocab prints) plus term:/phrase:/relation: ids, resolves each whole — definition, aliases, anchors — and joins phrasings via the terms: back-reference and relations via from/to, with contrasts-with edges separated from the rest because asking for both ends of one is a design error rather than a phrasing error. Partial results on a miss, exit 1 so a caller can tell a silent miss from a hit. Measured: two terms fully resolved = 1.56k tok; typical term ~780 tok; worst case client-llm 4.4k tok (41 phrasings, 39 edges) — follow-up filed for --brief. 6 tests; full suite 149 passed.

title: ./ch vocab: the register vocabulary index
description:
The detection surface for the reference guardrail. Prints every term a register names — slug, canonical term, kind — one line each, for a target expression (default: all mounted registers).

Measured: 430 BAML terms = 2,853 tokens; all three mounted registers ~3,900. Cheap enough to load into an agent's context whole, which is the point — the agent decides relevance by READING the vocabulary rather than querying it.

Read-only. Follows the ask/where conventions: target grammar via resolve.py, --json for programmatic use.
design: Terms only, not phrasebook. Measured phrase-only for BAML is 8,526 tok (3x the term index). Phrasebook entries carry a terms: back-reference and relations carry from/to, so both JOIN to the selected terms deterministically in the evaluation pass — they never need to be loaded up front.
acceptance_criteria: ./ch vocab prints all mounted registers; ./ch vocab <corpus>/<vN> scopes to one; --json emits structured output; tests cover both; no writes.
close_reason: ./ch vocab lands: register vocabulary index, grouped in corpus group order, with --json carrying the join keys (slug, kind, group, defined_in) for ./ch entry. Validated against the four novice prompts that broke embedding retrieval — schema-aligned-parsing, pdf-type, usage/collector, b-stream/semantic-streaming are all plainly readable in the index, 4/4 of what search missed. Measured output: 12-factor-agents/v1 1.6k tok, boundaryml-baml/v1 5.4k tok, all three registers 7.2k tok. 6 tests in test_interaction.py; full suite 143 passed.

title: Redefinition gate holds unvalidated payloads, so an accepted gate can fail to apply
description:
A payload held for the redefinition gate is written to work/authoring/gated/ without ever being validated. It is validated only when the human accepts the gate and ./ch set runs. So the gate can present a decision whose accept branch cannot be executed, and the human has no way to know that when deciding.

Observed repeatedly in the 149-chapter authoring run for boundaryml-baml/v1. Of 8 gate rows accepted by the user, 3 could not be applied at all, and 2 of those failed on a single trivial schema violation that then cascaded into a dozen misleading follow-on errors:

  baml-basics/04    terms[1]: 'definition' is 410 chars (max 400)
                    -> lexicon rejected -> 7 further errors, all of the form
                       "term 'b-stream' is not in the lexicon - author the lexicon
                       entry first", which are pure consequences of the lexicon
                       not having applied, not independent defects

  prompt-syntax/03  terms[9].anchors[0]: 'quote' must be a single line
                    -> lexicon rejected -> 6 further cascade errors

  language-reference/10  4x quote not found (genuine, and it did need re-authoring)

The user had already answered the gate for all three. The accept command printed by --apply simply failed, and the only recovery is to re-author the chapter from scratch, which discards the human decision and re-opens the same gate on the next pass. baml-basics/04 and prompt-syntax/03 each went through three authoring passes for this reason.

This compounds with chiron-t11: because the failure surfaces through ./ch set rather than through --apply, the violations never reach failures.json, so ./ch author --retry cannot feed them back either.
design: The gate currently sits before validation in the apply path. Moving validation ahead of the hold decision would mean an invalid payload never reaches a human: it becomes an ordinary rejection, gets its violations stored, and --retry can fix it and re-present the gate on the next apply. That also preserves the human decision, since the gate would then only ever be raised on material that is ready to write.
acceptance_criteria: A payload is schema-validated before it is written to gated/ and offered at the redefinition gate. Either the gate refuses to hold an invalid payload (routing the chapter to the normal REJECTED/retry path with its violations recorded in failures.json instead), or --apply prints the validation status alongside each gate so the human knows the accept branch is executable before choosing. Accepting a gate should never fail on a schema violation that was knowable at hold time.

title: camelCase and dotted identifiers never match their lexicon slugs
description:
study._norm() strips punctuation without splitting on case or dots, so a developer pasting a real symbol matches nothing.

  term: llm.determineNextStep   kind: identifier
  'determine next step'  -> term:determine-next-step (slug)   MATCHES
  'determinenextstep'    -> None                              MISSES
  'b.DetermineNextStep(' -> None                              MISSES

Identifiers are the highest-precision detection signal available — an exact symbol name is unambiguous evidence the prompt concerns this corpus — and they are the largest term kind: 239 of 430 in boundaryml-baml/v1 (56%), 39 of 131 in 12-factor-agents/v1 (30%).

Affects surface_forms(), and therefore both ./ch grade coverage and any exact-match channel in the guardrail.
design: Split camelCase/PascalCase boundaries and dots into word breaks when normalizing BOTH the stored surface form and the query, so llm.determineNextStep, DetermineNextStep and determine-next-step all normalize alike. Watch for collisions with existing single-word forms before landing.
acceptance_criteria: A prompt containing DetermineNextStep or b.DetermineNextStep(...) matches term:determine-next-step; existing surface-form tests still pass; no new cross-register collisions.

title: boundaryml-baml/v1: 22 duplicate-sense slug groups across the lexicon (45 of 430 slugs)
description:
The 149-chapter authoring run reproduced, at register scale, the same defect that chiron-jc4 records for the introduction group: two or more slugs for one concept, with the identical term string and kind.

Cause is structural, not an author error. Every chapter in a Batch API run is authored in parallel against the SAME lexicon slug index, so no chapter can see what any other chapter in its batch is minting. Seeding the index first (the introduction group was authored and deduped before this run) demonstrably helped — all 26 seed slugs were reused, and the class/function/prompt pairs did not come back — but it cannot prevent collisions AMONG the 149 chapters of a single batch.

Auto-demotion does not catch these because it only resolves exact slug collisions. Two different slugs for one term are invisible to it, and every affected chapter reports ok forever, because ok only means anchors are pinned to the current content_hash.

Cost: the concept-relations graph is split across both members of each pair, and future chapters will attract references to whichever member they happen to encounter. Two examples already observed in the wild: relations.yaml carries BOTH 'base-url --configures--> openai-generic-provider' (chapter 22) and 'base-url-option --configures--> openai-generic-provider' (chapter 09), the same assertion under two names; and 'test' has fractured three ways.

Full inventory follows.
430 terms, 22 duplicate-sense groups covering 45 slugs.

  /_debug/ping (identifier)
      debug-ping                         defined_in development/06
      debug-ping-endpoint                defined_in installation-language/06
  @@dynamic (identifier)
      dynamic-attribute                  defined_in baml-basics/03
      dynamic-class-attribute            defined_in language-reference/14
  _.role() (identifier)
      role-helper                        defined_in prompt-syntax/05
      underscore-role                    defined_in baml-advanced/04
  add_baml (identifier)
      add-baml                           defined_in baml-advanced/03
      add-baml-method                    defined_in generated-baml-client/06
  api_key (identifier)
      api-key-field                      defined_in language-reference/02
      api-key-option                     defined_in llm-client-providers/03
  audio (identifier)
      audio-class                        defined_in baml-basics/05

design: Re-author the losing chapter of each pair SEQUENTIALLY, never as one batch - a batch would recreate the parallel-blind condition that caused this. ch set re-applies a chapter's entries wholesale, so dropping a slug from the payload of its only defining chapter retires it; re-author all three dimensions per chapter so relations and phrasebook do not dangle. Where both members are anchored by many chapters (base_url, api_key, test), retiring one means re-authoring every chapter that references it, so those are the expensive ones - consider whether the pair is genuinely one sense first. Note ch author --retry cannot carry this finding (chiron-t11); the working path is the ch:lingua-author subagent writing a payload applied via ch set, which is how chiron-jc4's three pairs were fixed.
acceptance_criteria: Each of the 22 groups resolves to one surviving slug, chosen by the methodology's step 4 rule (the canonical surface form the corpus itself writes). No relation or phrasebook entry references a retired slug. ./ch status shows every affected chapter still ok afterwards.

title: Shared lexicon/phrasebook entry content is last-writer-wins across chapters, silently
description:
A lexicon or phrasebook entry can be anchored by many chapters, but its CONTENT (definition, intent, template) has a single stored value. Applying a chapter's payload rewrites that shared content wholesale. So authoring or re-authoring one chapter can silently degrade the rendered page of every other chapter that shares the entry, and nothing reports it: all the affected chapters stay 'ok', because ok only means every anchor is pinned to its chapter's current content_hash.

Found by ch:lingua-validator on boundaryml-baml/v1/llm-client-providers/16. The phrase slug use-openai-generic-with-overridden-base-url is shared by five chapters:

  llm-client-providers/12  Groq
  llm-client-providers/15  Llama API
  llm-client-providers/16  LiteLLM
  llm-client-providers/20  Tinfoil
  llm-client-providers/21  Together AI

Re-authoring chapter 16 rewrote the shared intent and template into LiteLLM-specific wording ('point a BAML client at a LiteLLM proxy through the OpenAI-compatible provider'). Chapter 16's own page reads correctly; the other four now render a phrase whose template names a vendor they have nothing to do with. Every one of the five still reports ok.

The redefinition gate protects exactly this for the DEFINING chapter of a lexicon term - it asks a human before ownership moves. There is no equivalent protection for the content of an entry that many chapters merely reference, and none at all for phrasebook entries.

This gets more likely as a register fills: the more chapters share vocabulary, the more often a later chapter's write lands on an entry an earlier chapter depends on. boundaryml-baml/v1 has 153 chapters over 430 terms and 446 phrases, so shared entries are the norm, not the exception.
design: The redefinition gate already has the shape needed: it detects that a payload changes something another chapter owns, and holds for a human. The gap is that it triggers only on lexicon define ownership. Extending the same comparison to entry CONTENT (and to phrasebook entries, which have no gate at all) would reuse the existing machinery. A lighter first step is report-only - print a 'narrowed shared entry' warning listing the other anchoring chapters - since not every shared-entry rewrite is a regression and gating all of them would be noisy.
acceptance_criteria: Rewriting the content of an entry that other chapters anchor is either surfaced or gated. Minimally, ./ch author --apply reports when an applied payload changes the stored content of an entry anchored by chapters outside the current run, naming them, so the orchestrator can judge whether the new wording still serves them.

title: boundaryml-baml/v1: dedup re-minted keyword slugs in the introduction group
description:
The first authoring batch for boundaryml-baml/v1/introduction (4 chapters, all submitted in one Batch API run) minted three concepts twice, because every chapter in a batch is authored in parallel against the SAME lexicon slug index — which was empty, this being the register's first run. Auto-demotion only resolves exact slug collisions, so two slugs for one concept slip through.

The duplicate pairs, all identical term string and kind:

  class-keyword    (introduction/01)  <-> class     (introduction/02)
  function-keyword (introduction/01)  <-> function  (introduction/02)
  prompt-keyword   (introduction/01)  <-> prompt    (introduction/02)

Independently confirmed by ch:lingua-validator on introduction/02 (three 'duplicate-sense' errors). Note the validator framed it as a methodology violation because it read the index as it stands now; at submit time the index was empty for all four chapters, so this is a parallel-batch artifact, not an author ignoring step 1.

It is already splitting the concept-relations graph: introduction/01 contributes 'baml-function-definition --uses--> class-keyword' while introduction/02 contributes edges on 'class'. Future chapters will attract references to whichever of the pair they happen to see first.

Related but separate findings from the same validation pass, worth fixing in the same re-authoring:
- introduction/02: the edge 'baml-client --feeds--> function' is inverted. The chapter states generation runs the other way ('BAML generates fully typed clients for all languages automatically'), corroborated by introduction/04 and /01. Should be function --feeds--> baml-client.
- introduction/03: the 'declaration' definition reads 'A BAML definition (such as a function, class, or client) placed within baml_src'. That six-sentence chapter contains no code and names none of the three; the enumeration is borrowed from introduction/01 and /02. Same class of defect as the rejection this chapter already had.
design: Pick the surviving slug first. Methodology step 4 says use the canonical surface form the corpus itself uses most, which favours class/function/prompt over the -keyword suffix the corpus never writes; the earlier-chapter-wins convention used by auto-demotion favours the introduction/01 entries. Whichever wins, re-author BOTH chapters SEQUENTIALLY, not as one batch — a single batch would recreate the parallel-blind condition that caused this. ch set re-applies a chapter's entries wholesale, so dropping a slug from the payload of its only defining chapter removes it; re-author all three dimensions per chapter so relations and phrasebook do not dangle on a removed slug.
acceptance_criteria: ./ch status shows introduction/01..04 ok across all three dimensions; the lexicon page lists exactly one slug per concept for class, function and prompt; no relation references a removed slug; the function/baml-client edge runs function --feeds--> baml-client; and introduction/03's declaration definition contains only claims grounded in that chapter.
notes:
PARTIALLY DONE (2026-09-10). The three keyword duplicates are resolved.

Kept the short slugs (class, function, prompt) per methodology step 4 — the corpus writes those forms and never writes 'class-keyword', and the rest of the lexicon is unsuffixed (enum, output-dir, retry-policy). All three doomed entries were defined_in introduction/01 and anchored only there, and the single outside reference was one relations edge, also 01's — so re-authoring introduction/01 alone was sufficient; introduction/02 already owned the survivors and was not touched.

Applied via the skill's agent-authored fallback path (ch:lingua-author -> scratchpad JSON -> ./ch set), because ./ch author --retry could not carry the finding — see chiron-t11. introduction/01 now emits 7 definitions plus mention-only entries for class/function/prompt, and its edge baml-function-definition --uses--> class-keyword was re-pointed to class. grep confirms zero occurrences of class-keyword/function-keyword/prompt-keyword across lexicon.yaml, phrasebook.yaml and relations.yaml; all four introduction chapters remain ok.

STILL OPEN in this issue:
1. introduction/02's inverted edge 'baml-client --feeds--> function' (should be function --feeds--> baml-client). Not fixed — out of scope for the dedup, and 02 was left untouched deliberately.
2. introduction/03's 'declaration' definition still carries the ungrounded parenthetical 'such as a function, class, or client'.

NEW near-duplicates surfaced by the re-authoring agent, same shape as the ones just fixed, both deliberately left alone:
3. client-keyword (introduction/01, the client field inside a function) vs client-llm (introduction/02, the client<llm> declaration block, which carries 'client' as an alias). Arguably two senses, but it is the same -keyword suffix pattern just retired, and chapter 01 never writes client<llm>. Merging would mean dropping the alias on client-llm; chapter 01 could then only offer a grounding stretch as a mention.
4. function (identifier, the keyword) vs baml-function-definition (concept, the declaration). Treated as distinct — the concept is genuinely introduction/01's — but worth a look once more of the corpus is authored and the usage pattern is visible.

title: No path from a lingua-validator verdict into author --retry feedback
description:
/ch:translate step 5 says a validator 'fail' verdict 'earns one more retry round inside the same cap', but no mechanism implements it.

tools/lingua/author.py build_params()/chapter_message() accept a feedback string, and it is genuinely useful — feeding the stored violations back is what turned boundaryml-baml/v1/introduction/03 from REJECTED into a clean apply on attempt 1. But the only producer of that string is retry(), which builds it from failures.json, and failures.json is written only by the --apply path's schema and anchor-verbatim validation. A ch:lingua-validator verdict is a JSON blob in an agent's final message that never touches the run directory.

Consequence: after a validator returns fail, ./ch author --retry <id> re-authors with feedback '(no stored violations)' plus the previous payload — i.e. blind. The orchestrator burns a retry from the 2-per-chapter cap on a request that carries no information about what was wrong, and will often reproduce the same defect. The only honest options today are to re-author blind or to stop and report, which is what this session did.

Observed on the first authored group of boundaryml-baml/v1 (introduction, 4 chapters). Both sampled validators returned fail with specific, actionable, correctly-grounded findings (an ungrounded enumeration in a definition, three re-minted duplicate slugs, one inverted relation direction) and none of it could be handed back to the author.
design: The feedback plumbing already exists end to end (build_params -> chapter_message). What is missing is a second writer into that channel besides the apply path's failures.json. Simplest shape is likely a new flag on retry() that merges an external verdict JSON into the feedback_lines it already builds per dimension, keeping failures.json as the schema/anchor channel and the verdict as the judgement channel.
acceptance_criteria: A ch:lingua-validator verdict can be fed into a re-authoring request, so the author sees the specific findings. E.g. ./ch author --retry <id> --from-verdict <verdict.json>, or a documented CLI path that records validator issues where retry() will pick them up. The 2-retry cap should count only informed retries.

title: author --status reports false HELD after a redefinition gate is resolved
description:
tools/lingua/author.py run_status() derives 'HELD (redefinition gate)' from the mere presence of files in work/authoring/gated/ (see the gated_keys set built from gate_dir.glob('*.json')). Nothing clears those files when the gate is actually resolved: 'ch set <dim> --from ...gated/<key>-lexicon.json --redefine' writes the data and a later 'ch author --apply' prints 'nothing rejected or held', but the gated/*.json files stay on disk, so 'ch author --status' keeps reporting HELD forever.

Observed on boundaryml-baml/v1/introduction/03: ./ch status shows lexicon ok, phrasebook ok, concept-relations ok, and --apply prints 'applied 1 chapter(s); nothing rejected or held', while --status prints 'attempts 0  HELD (redefinition gate)'. run.json itself is clean (attempts 0, parked null) - the false state comes only from the leftover gated/ files.

This matters because /ch:translate's report and /ch:verify both read the retry/held columns from --status rather than from memory, so a resolved gate looks unresolved to the next session.
acceptance_criteria: After a redefinition gate is resolved (accept or reject branch), ./ch author --status no longer reports HELD for that chapter. Either 'ch set --redefine'/'--from ...demoted.json' removes that chapter's gated/*.json, or --apply clears them once the chapter's dimensions validate, or run_status cross-checks the chapter's actual dimension states before trusting gated/.
notes:
Two call sites share the root cause, both testing only for file presence in work/authoring/gated/:

  tools/lingua/author.py  run_status()   -> gated_keys from gate_dir.glob('*.json')  -> 'HELD (redefinition gate)'
  tools/lingua/where.py:52 _run_state()  -> held = gated.is_dir() and any(gated.glob('*.json'))  -> next_action() returns '/ch:translate <reg>   (redefinition gate open)'

The where.py path is the more damaging of the two: GRAMMAR.md requires every skill's report to reproduce the ./ch where state line byte-identical, so a resolved gate makes every subsequent report advertise a gate that is not open, and sends the reader to /ch:translate instead of the real next action. On boundaryml-baml/v1 the line currently reads:

  boundaryml-baml/v1 · 153 chapters · lexicon 4 ok, 149 none · phrasebook 4 ok, 149 none · concept-relations 4 ok, 149 none · next: /ch:translate boundaryml-baml/v1   (redefinition gate open)

when the correct next action is /ch:translate against the next unauthored group. Whatever clears the state must fix both call sites - ideally by deleting the chapter's gated/*.json once its dimensions validate, so the presence test stays honest rather than being replaced by a second inference.

title: ./ch entry --brief: cap the joins for hot terms
description:
A hot term resolves large: boundaryml-baml/v1's client-llm carries 41 phrasings and 39 edges, 17.6k chars (~4.4k tokens) for one entry. baml-client is 10.5k chars, function 8.4k. Typical terms are ~780 tokens, so this only bites on the handful of terms that everything else hangs off.

Uncapped is the right default — silently dropping a phrasing or an edge would undercut the one thing the surface can honestly promise, that what it did not list the register does not hold. But a caller assembling a guardrail context from several hot terms may want the definition plus counts without every gloss.

--brief: keep definition, aliases, anchors and the relation TYPES with counts; drop the glosses and the phrasing bodies. --json stays uncapped regardless.

title: boundaryml-baml/v1/llm-client-providers/16 parked: author cannot produce verbatim anchors
description:
Parked during the 149-chapter authoring run for boundaryml-baml/v1 after exhausting both retries. All three dimensions remain 'none'.

The chapter is fern/03-reference/baml/clients/providers/litellm.mdx — 361 bytes, essentially a pointer page saying LiteLLM works through the openai-generic provider with an overridden base_url.

Both attempts failed the same way, on anchor quotes that were not verbatim:

  terms[0] 'litellm'
    author quote: Set up LiteLLM Proxy server
    source text:  Set up [LiteLLM Proxy server](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/docker_quick_start#21-start-proxy)
    -> the Markdown link syntax was stripped

  terms[1] 'openai-generic'
    author quote: an\novervridden base_url.
    source text:  with an\noverridden base_url.
    -> 'overridden' transcribed as 'overvridden', a typo introduced by the author and not present in the source

Neither is a grounding failure — the author picked the right sentences both times. It is a transcription problem, the same markup-stripping and mis-copying class that caused most rejections in this run (22 of 37 rejection lines across the run were quote-not-found).

Low priority: the page carries almost no vocabulary of its own; its entire content redirects to llm-client-providers/openai-generic, which is authored and ok.
acceptance_criteria: Either boundaryml-baml/v1/llm-client-providers/16 reaches ok on all three dimensions, or a deliberate decision is recorded that this pointer page should be excluded from the register via the adapter's exclude knob (note: excluding one page inside a group renumbers that group and orphans its anchors, so prefer authoring it).
close_reason:
Resolved. A fresh authoring run (not a retry) produced a clean payload that applied on the first attempt with zero retries; boundaryml-baml/v1/llm-client-providers/16 is now ok on lexicon, phrasebook and concept-relations.

The /ch:verify workup classified both prior failures as paraphrase rather than hallucination: five of seven quotes matched the chapter, and the two that failed were near-misses in the same page (Markdown link syntax stripped; 'overridden' mistyped as 'overvridden'). The decisive evidence was that the same failing payload already carried 'an overridden base_url' as a PASSING anchor on the base-url term — the author could render the span correctly and had done so one entry earlier. That made a third pass worth spending rather than leaving the chapter parked.

Confirms the general lesson: a fresh run beats a retry once failures.json has been cleared, because --retry then re-authors blind with '(no stored violations)'. See chiron-t11.

title: docgen: Rust support once rustdoc JSON stabilizes
description: Excluded deliberately at plan time: cargo doc --output-format json is nightly-only and the rustdoc-JSON-to-Markdown converters are immature. BAML (corpora/boundaryml-baml, an empty incomplete mount) is the motivating corpus — its Rust core would chapter from its TS/Python bindings until this lands.

title: docgen: add doxide as a second C/C++ path
description: Doxide emits Markdown natively and avoids the doxygen->XML->moxygen hop, but needs a source build (cmake, libclang, yaml-cpp, ICU) the image does not carry. Left out of the closed TOOLS registry rather than listed-and-broken. Worth adding if the moxygen path proves limiting on a real C++ corpus.

title: docgen: manifest v7 for generation provenance
description: A generated chapter is indistinguishable from a written one in the viewer. Corpus.generated_by exists and reaches the extract bundle, but is deliberately not in the manifest: adding it means bumping manifest.py VERSION and the !== 6 guard in web/lib/content.ts together, and there is no viewer surface to show it yet. Deferred at plan time with the user's agreement (substrate-only, no web/ changes). Revisit if the viewer ever grows a provenance line or a reading pane.

title: Regenerate design/ui-map.json as-built after the ui-map-1 viewer landed
description: The as-built UI map describes the retired Reeder shell + bit modal. Per design/README's maintenance note, regenerate it from the new implementation (rail|index|entry shell, entry routes, overlays), recording the deliberate deviations: drill is overlay-only (no /drill route), IJKL/EDAF bindings retired, o-key opens source_url only (a bare source path has no useful browser target).

title: render.py: escape raw angle-bracket tokens in injected prose
description: Lexicon definitions (e.g. event_to_prompt's '<type>...</type> tags') flow into pages/*.md unescaped, where any markdown renderer with a raw-HTML pass parses them as elements. The web viewer now literalizes unknown tags (web/components/MarkdownArticle.tsx rehypeLiteralUnknowns), but the generator should still markdown-escape '<' in definition/intent prose it writes into Terms/Phrasings sections and pages/lexicon.md so other consumers render it correctly too.

title: Keep methodology schema sections in lockstep with validate_payload
description: methodology/<slug>.md '## Schema and caps' restates each dimension's validate_payload; code is source of truth. Check on every dimension change.

title: Viewer: peek on index rows
description: design/ui-map-1.json open question 3: space-peek currently works only on entry cross-references. Extending it to index rows (preview without opening) is cheap — the peek already resolves any entry from the substrate — but might make the entry pane feel optional; decide deliberately.

title: Codetree granularity heuristics
description: Depth-2 directory chaptering is deterministic but crude for monorepos (one huge src/ dir becomes one chapter). Smarter clustering out of v1 scope; adapter include/exclude/depth knobs are the mitigation.
